title: Lamport clocks: ordering events when no two clocks agree
dek: In 1978 Leslie Lamport showed that machines don't need to agree on the time to agree on the order of events. Count instead of timing, send the count with every message, and a cause always gets a smaller number than its effect. Every replicated database still leans on this idea.

items: Clocks on different machines disagree by milliseconds or more, so sorting events by their timestamps can put an effect before its cause.

Lamport's fix: forget real time. Each machine counts its events, every message carries the count, and a machine that receives a message jumps its count past the one it received. A cause always gets a smaller number than its effect.

Break ties by machine name and every machine sorts the same events into the same order. Run the same commands in the same order on every copy and the copies stay identical: the idea under every replicated database.

body.x: The paper: "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System" by Leslie Lamport, Communications of the ACM, July 1978. It is one of the most cited papers in computer science, and his 2013 Turing Award citation names causality and logical clocks first.

A restaurant marks paneer tikka sold out. The menu server records it, and its clock says 12:00:00.500, but that clock runs 300 ms fast. The order server hears about it, and a moment later refuses a customer's order for paneer tikka; its clock says 12:00:00.260. Weeks later, support sorts the logs by time to answer a complaint. The refusal comes first, before the dish was sold out, and the log now says Zotato refused an order for no reason.

items: Every machine's clock drifts. Time sync keeps servers within a few milliseconds of each other on a good day and further apart on a bad one, and phones can be off by seconds.
A clock can jump backwards when it is corrected, so even one machine's timestamps can go out of order.
Messages take a different time each trip, so the time an event is received says little about when it happened.

body.x: Lamport asked a different question. Not "what time was it?" but "could this event have affected that one?" That question has an exact answer, and machines can track it without any clock at all.

items: On one machine, an earlier event happened before a later one.
Sending a message happened before receiving it.
Chains count: if A happened before B and B before C, then A happened before C.

body.x: If neither of two events happened before the other, they are concurrent: no message could have carried news of one to the other, so neither could have affected the other, and any order between them is equally true.
Two letters posted in different cities on the same day have no meaningful "which came first". But a reply can never be written before the letter it answers, whatever the postmarks say.

items: Each machine keeps a counter that starts at 0.
Before each event (a change, a send, a receive) it adds 1, and the event gets that number.
Every message carries the sender's number. On receiving one, the machine sets its counter to the bigger of its own and the message's, then adds 1.

body.label: Lamport clock
body.x:
on a local event:    clock = clock + 1
on sending message:  clock = clock + 1;  message.count = clock
on receiving it:     clock = max(clock, message.count) + 1
body.say: On a local event, add one to the clock. On sending a message, add one and put the clock in the message. On receiving one, take the bigger of your clock and the message's count, and add one.

body.cap: The menu server is at 6 when it marks paneer tikka sold out, so that event is 7, and the 7 travels with the update. The order server was at 3; it takes max(3, 7) + 1 = 8 for receiving it and 9 for refusing the order, and tells the support log, which becomes 10. By count the sold-out comes first. By wall clock the refusal looks 240 ms earlier.

body.x: That is the whole mechanism: a number and a max. No clock sync, no central server. The receiver's jump is what guarantees that anything caused by the message gets a bigger number than the message itself.
What the numbers promise, and what they don't

body.label: What a Lamport count tells you
head: If
Then
rows: A's number is smaller than B's
A may have caused B, or they may be unrelated
Two events on different machines have the same number
They are unrelated; break the tie by machine name

body.x: The promise runs one way. That is enough to sort events so that causes come first, but not to tell whether two events were concurrent. To detect that two people edited the same cart on two servers without seeing each other's change, systems keep one counter per machine, a vector clock. Other researchers added it about ten years later, building on this paper.

Break ties by machine name and every pair of events has a winner, so every machine sorts the same events into the same list, whatever order they arrived in. The paper uses this to share one resource without a lock server: each request is stamped, sent to every machine, and served in that agreed order.

body.cap: Two customers try to hold seat 14 at the same moment, on machines A and C, and both requests are stamped 5. Each machine receives the three requests in a different order, sorts by count and then by machine name, and ends with the same list. Every copy gives seat 14 to A's customer.

body.x: The same pages hold a bigger idea. If every copy of a service runs the same commands in the same order, every copy ends in the same state. That is state machine replication, the base of replicated databases and of consensus protocols such as Raft (see the Consensus concept).

items: Sequence numbers on chat messages, so everyone in a conversation sees the same order (the Chat problem).
Terms in leader election: a message from a newer term always wins over an older one (the Consensus concept).
Version numbers on database rows, so a write based on an old version is refused instead of silently overwriting a newer one.
Vector clocks in key-value stores that accept writes on several machines, to find conflicting edits (the Key-value store problem).
Hybrid clocks in globally spread databases: wall-clock time plus a counter, so numbers stay close to real time but never go backwards.
When order across servers matters (chat messages, edits, events), say you won't sort by server timestamps, and why: clocks drift and jump.
Give one order per conversation or per key: a sequence number from that partition's leader, or a logical clock.
If you must detect concurrent edits, not just order them, name vector clocks, and say how conflicts get resolved: last write wins quietly loses data; merging or asking the user doesn't.
Keep wall-clock time for showing to people, not for deciding order.

body.label: Go deeper: what the paper says about real clocks

body.x: Counts only know about messages inside the system. If you phone a friend and they then place an order, the system never saw the call, so it may put their order before your action. The second half of the paper handles this with physical clocks: if every clock drifts by at most a known rate and machines exchange times often enough, clocks can be kept within a known bound of each other, and events further apart than that bound are ordered correctly.

The shared-resource example assumes every message arrives, in order, and that every machine answers. One slow or dead machine stalls everyone. Real systems keep the idea of one agreed order but use majorities so they can carry on when some machines fail; that is what consensus protocols add.
